title: Can and could for ability and requests
objectives: Form negatives and questions with can and could.
Make requests using can or could.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Use can to talk about an ability now: something a person knows how to do or is able to do. ‘I can swim’ means that swimming is an ability I have. ‘My sister can speak French’ tells us about her ability. Can also describes what is possible in a situation: ‘We can use this room today’ means that the room is available for us to use.

Use could for a general ability in the past: ‘When I was seven, I could ride a bicycle.’ Could does not always describe one successful action at a particular time. For a single completed success, English often uses another expression, such as ‘managed to’. This unit focuses on general ability and polite requests.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Can and could are modal verbs. A modal verb is a helping verb that adds a meaning such as ability. Use the same form with every subject: I can, she can and they can; he could and we could. Put the base form of the main verb after the modal: ‘She can play’, not ‘She can plays’. Do not add to between the modal and the verb.

To make a negative, use cannot or can’t, and could not or couldn’t: ‘I can’t swim’ and ‘He couldn’t read at age three’. Cannot is usually written as one word. To make a yes/no question, put can or could before the subject: ‘Can you drive?’ A short answer uses the modal: ‘Yes, I can’ or ‘No, I can’t’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Use ‘Can you …?’ to ask someone to do something: ‘Can you open the window?’ ‘Could you …?’ is another common way to make a request and often sounds more polite. The word please can make the request more courteous: ‘Could you help me, please?’ Your tone and situation also affect how polite a request sounds.

Read the examples below. In ‘Could you pass me the salt?’, could introduces a present request, not a question about the past. In ‘I could swim when I was six’, could describes a past ability. Context helps you understand which meaning the speaker intends.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use do or does to form a question with can: say ‘Can she drive?’, not ‘Does she can drive?’ Do not add an -s to the main verb after can or could: say ‘He can cook’. Also distinguish ability from permission. ‘Can I sit here?’ can ask for permission; ‘Can you sit here?’ often asks the listener to do something.

Both can and could are possible in many requests. Could often sounds less direct, but neither word is automatically polite in every situation. With a positive short answer, use the full modal form: ‘Yes, she can’, not ‘Yes, she can’t’, which gives a negative answer.
